_meta.title: Recommendation pilot — everyday AI assistants
_meta.purpose: One category, thirteen alternatives, nine criteria. Feeds the preview at /recommend. Not a general scoring layer and no aggregate score.
_meta.provenance_note: A model read each source; no human re-read them. Nothing is marked human-reviewed.

identity_model.why: Three different things get confused when a product is described by one 'provider'. They answer different questions and must be applied only to the question they can answer.
identity_model.product_provider: Who operates the consumer product. Governance criteria attach here.
identity_model.model_provider: Whose model serves it. May differ from the product provider, and may vary by surface.
identity_model.model_release: Which specific model version. Licensing criteria attach here.
identity_model.rule: Unknown model routing does NOT invalidate an established product-provider identity, nor any provider-level governance finding. It only leaves model-level questions unanswered.

status_separation.retrieval_status: Whether we could fetch the source. 'blocked' means a server refused an automated request — it is not evidence about the product.
status_separation.factual_status: Whether the fact is established, and from what kind of source.
status_separation.rule: A retrieval failure is recorded separately from factual uncertainty and never presented as doubt about the product.

claim_types.established_outcome: Recorded in a filing, licence, index, court record or official product documentation.
claim_types.company_statement: The company's own description of itself.
claim_types.allegation: Claimed by a party to a dispute, not settled.

status_values.proposed: Reported or announced, not established as in force.

decision_rules.soft_by_default: A preference explains and orders. It never excludes, and an unknown preference neither rewards nor penalises.
decision_rules.hard_opt_in: A criterion excludes only when the user explicitly designates it a requirement, and only where the evidence can decide.
decision_rules.unknown_requirement: An unknown hard requirement is never shown as satisfied. The option goes to a separate 'requirement not confirmed' group — visible, not shortlisted, not excluded.
decision_rules.no_filling: Shortlist slots are never filled to reach a number.

corrections_applied: Anthropic’s statement that exported data cannot be imported into another personal Claude account is account-to-account evidence. It no longer drives cross-service migration, which is a different question with a different destination.
Cross-service migration is unconfirmed for every option until evidence addresses the destination product and what must transfer.
A requirement is never downgraded to a preference because evidence is missing. It stays a requirement and returns an explicit unconfirmed state.
Criterion labels are written to be understood on their own; the scope caveats sit in an evidence section rather than in front of the label.

criteria.label: No single person holds more than half the votes
criteria.concept: Whether any single person holds more than 50% of the votes.
criteria.does_not_establish: That no individual controls the company, or that no one can override the board. Control can also run through board seats, class rights, supermajority provisions or contract. We only report the voting-power figure.
criteria.distinct_from: Founder-bloc voting power. Two founders with 52.7% between them is not one founder with 52.7%.
criteria.plain: Whether one person could outvote everyone else.

criteria.label: The founders together hold less than half the votes
criteria.concept: Whether founders acting together hold more than 50% of the votes.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the founders act together in practice, or that they control the company by other means. A bloc requires its members to agree.
criteria.distinct_from: Any single individual's voting power.
criteria.plain: Whether the founders, voting as a group, could outvote everyone else.

criteria.label: Who can appoint and remove the board
criteria.concept: Which party can elect or remove directors, separately from economic ownership.
criteria.does_not_establish: Day-to-day operational control.
criteria.distinct_from: Voting power over ordinary resolutions.
criteria.plain: We have findings on this, but there is no single better answer to prefer — the arrangements differ in kind, not in degree.

criteria.label: A legal duty to weigh more than shareholder returns
criteria.concept: A legal structure currently obliging the company to weigh non-shareholder interests.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the obligation has changed any decision.
criteria.distinct_from: Commitment continuity — whether earlier commitments were kept.
criteria.plain: A company structure that currently obliges directors to consider people other than shareholders.

criteria.label: Past public-benefit promises have been kept
criteria.concept: Whether public-benefit mechanisms this provider adopted have been kept or withdrawn.
criteria.does_not_establish: What the provider will do next.
criteria.distinct_from: What is in force now.
criteria.plain: Whether commitments of this kind, once adopted, were later withdrawn.

criteria.label: You can download your own conversations
criteria.concept: Whether you can download your conversations and account data from the product.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the export can be used anywhere else.
criteria.distinct_from: Migrating to another service, which needs somewhere to import it.
criteria.plain: A way to get your chat history and account data out of the product.

criteria.label: You can move your content to another account with the same provider
criteria.plain: Transferring your history from one account to another at the same company.
criteria.concept: Whether exported content can be loaded into a different account at the same provider.
criteria.does_not_establish: Anything about moving to a different company’s product. A provider can refuse account-to-account transfer and still place no obstacle in front of taking your data elsewhere.
criteria.distinct_from: Cross-service migration, which is about a different destination entirely.

criteria.label: You can move your content to a different company’s product
criteria.concept: Whether exported content can be imported into a competing product and used there.
criteria.does_not_establish: Anything about model portability, and nothing about transfers within the same provider.
criteria.distinct_from: Account-to-account transfer at the same provider, which has a different destination and different evidence.
criteria.plain: Taking your history out of one product and using it in a competitor’s.
criteria.requires_evidence_about: Both the destination product and what actually has to transfer for the move to be useful.

criteria.label: You could run the model yourself
criteria.concept: Whether the specific model serving the product is published under a licence letting you run it yourself.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the hosted assistant is portable, or that your content comes with you.
criteria.distinct_from: Export and migration, which are about your data, not the model.
criteria.plain: Whether the model serving this product is published under a licence letting you host it.

criteria.label: Your conversations are not used for model training unless you allow it
criteria.plain: Whether your chats feed the provider's next model without you asking for that.
criteria.concept: Default position on training, before the user changes any setting.
criteria.does_not_establish: Anything about retention, human review, or use for advertising and product analytics, which are separate and often continue regardless.
criteria.distinct_from: Whether you can switch training off, which is the next question and has a different answer for several providers.

criteria.label: You can stay out of model training without contacting support
criteria.plain: Whether staying out is something you can do yourself, or something you have to ask for.
criteria.concept: Practical user control over the training outcome, by any route the user can take alone.
criteria.does_not_establish: That opting out removes data already used, or that it covers uses other than model training.
criteria.distinct_from: The default. A provider can train by default and still give you a switch.

criteria.label: What kind of owner sits behind the product
criteria.plain: Background on the kind of company behind the product. The specific things you can act on are the three questions above.
criteria.concept: The ownership shape of the operating company.
criteria.does_not_establish: That any shape is better than another, or anything about where your money ends up.
criteria.distinct_from: Voting arrangements, which describe who decides rather than who owns.
criteria.context_note: Shown as background. The shapes overlap — a company can be listed and founder-controlled at once — so this is not a single choice. Pick the precise questions above instead.

criteria.label: A foundation or non-profit holds control of the company
criteria.plain: Whether a body with a public purpose — not shareholders or a founder — decides who runs it.
criteria.concept: Where board-level control sits.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the foundation receives any money. Control and financial benefit are separate, and at least one provider here has one without the other.
criteria.distinct_from: Whether a non-profit holds an economic stake, which is the next question.

criteria.label: A public-purpose body has a documented economic stake or revenue share
criteria.plain: Whether a public-purpose organisation holds a financial interest in the business or has a documented right to a share of revenue.
criteria.concept: Documented economic participation by a public-purpose body.
criteria.does_not_establish: That any money has actually been paid. An ownership interest, a right to a share of revenue, and an actual payment are three different things and are recorded separately in the evidence.
criteria.distinct_from: A public-benefit duty, which obliges directors to weigh other interests but distributes nothing.

criteria.label: The operator is not a subsidiary of a larger commercial group
criteria.plain: Whether the company you pay answers to a bigger corporate owner.
criteria.concept: Whether a larger commercial parent sits above the operator.
criteria.does_not_establish: Anything about size or influence. A company can have no parent and still be one of the largest firms in the world.
criteria.distinct_from: Investor stakes. A large minority investor is not a parent.

criteria.label: I can take a copy of my project code out of the tool
criteria.plain: A documented route to get the code itself onto your own machine or repository.
criteria.concept: A documented code export or repository route.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the running app moves with it. Databases, stored files, secrets, sign-in providers and hosting are separate, and are asked about separately.
criteria.distinct_from: Hosting the app elsewhere, which needs somewhere for the code to run.

criteria.label: There is a documented way to host my app elsewhere
criteria.plain: A described route to run the finished app somewhere other than the tool that built it.
criteria.concept: A described external-hosting route for the generated app.
criteria.does_not_establish: That migration is effortless or complete. What carries over — database records, stored files, secrets, authentication — is stated per finding.
criteria.distinct_from: Code export. Having the code is not the same as having somewhere it runs.

criteria.label: My prompts and code are not used for training unless I opt in
criteria.plain: What happens by default, before you change any setting.
criteria.concept: Default treatment of prompts and generated code for the stated plan, region and account context.
criteria.does_not_establish: That training has or has not actually occurred. Permission in terms is evidence about permitted use, not a record of use.
criteria.distinct_from: Whether you can switch it off, which several providers allow even where the default is on.

criteria.label: I can stop training use through a setting
criteria.plain: Whether staying out is something you can do yourself, and what it covers.
criteria.concept: An evidenced self-service control, or no training use for the stated context.
criteria.does_not_establish: That the default already satisfies you, or that the control reaches content already used or contributed by collaborators.
criteria.distinct_from: The default position, which is asked separately.

criteria.label: I can move the app’s database and services too
criteria.plain: Whether the data and backend behind the app can move, not just the code.
criteria.concept: A documented route for the database, stored files, secrets and authentication.
criteria.does_not_establish: That a move is quick or complete. Sign-in providers and live sessions usually need reconfiguring wherever you go.
criteria.distinct_from: Hosting the app elsewhere, which can be true while the data stays put.

assessments.claim: Lovable documents hosting the built app elsewhere. Older React + Vite apps produce “static files that any static host can serve”, deployable to AWS, GCP, Azure, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages or self-hosted infrastructure. TanStack Start apps “run server code, such as server-side rendering, server functions, and API routes”, and need a host that supports server execution.
assessments.source: Lovable docs — deployment, hosting and ownership; external deployment and hosting
assessments.scope: Database, storage and configuration are described as portable to managed or self-hosted Supabase; moving to a different database provider requires code changes. A database export can include accounts and password hashes, but sign-in providers need reconfiguring and existing sessions do not carry over. The Lovable platform itself cannot be self-hosted.
assessments.uncertainty: A scoped route, not effortless migration. The app type changes which hosts will work.
assessments.plain: Yes — static apps run on any static host; newer server-rendered apps need a host that runs server code.
assessments.condition: Which hosts work depends on whether your app is React + Vite or TanStack Start.

assessments.claim: Replit describes code leaving as standard, uncompiled source with no proprietary format and no custom runtime dependency, via zip export, GitHub sync or SSH from a local IDE, and documents deploying to external cloud providers including AWS, Azure and GCP.

assessments.plain: Yes — take the code out by zip, GitHub or SSH and deploy it on your own cloud.

assessments.condition: Only if you have not already published to Bolt hosting. Bolt states there is no going back: you would need a new, unpublished copy.

assessments.claim: The v0 pricing page states “Training opt-out by default” for Business and “Your data is never used for training” for Enterprise. Free and Plus say nothing about training. Vercel’s AI policy describes defaults using different account labels — Hobby, trial Pro, paid Pro and Enterprise — which do not map onto v0’s subscription tiers.

assessments.scope: Business and Enterprise are documented on the v0 pricing page. Free and Plus are not, and the Vercel account labels are not assumed to correspond to them.
assessments.uncertainty: Two official sources describe plan tiers differently. Recorded as a source conflict rather than an unresearched gap, and not resolved by guessing which label means which.

free.claim: The v0 pricing page does not mention training for Free. Vercel’s AI policy uses different account labels that cannot be mapped to it with confidence.

business.claim: The v0 pricing page lists “Training opt-out by default” for Business.

enterprise.claim: The v0 pricing page states for Enterprise that “Your data is never used for training”.

assessments.plain: Business and Enterprise exclude your content by default. For Free and Plus the published pages disagree, so we have not settled it.
assessments.condition: Depends which plan you are on, and two official pages conflict.

assessments.claim: Lovable documents an account-level opt-out toggle, free of charge and applying going forward.
assessments.scope: The toggle covers that account user’s own contributions. It does not cover every collaborator’s contributions, and it is prospective rather than retroactive. The documentation says changes apply from 9 September 2026.
assessments.uncertainty: Provider statement, read directly. Automated research, not human-reviewed.
assessments.plain: Yes — an account toggle turns it off, going forward.
assessments.condition: It covers your own contributions, not every collaborator’s.

assessments.claim: Replit documents the path Settings → Personalization → Opt out of Model Improvement, and says that once opted out, “new content associated with your account will not be used to develop or improve our models.” The documentation addresses Pro and Enterprise; Starter and Core are not covered.
assessments.scope: Even after opting out, Replit states it may still process content to provide, maintain, secure and troubleshoot the service, enforce its terms and comply with law.
assessments.uncertainty: Documented for Pro; not established for Starter or Core. Choosing a plan below resolves it.

starter.claim: The model-improvement documentation does not address Starter.

core.claim: The model-improvement documentation does not address Core.

pro.claim: Pro users can opt out at Settings → Personalization → Model Improvement. The opt-out applies to new content.

enterprise.claim: Replit states Enterprise customer content is not used to train its models, so there is nothing to switch off.

assessments.plain: On Pro, turn it off at Settings → Personalization → Model Improvement. Enterprise content is not used at all. Starter and Core are not covered by the documentation we read.

assessments.claim: StackBlitz states you may opt out of the model-development and dataset-licensing uses “at any time, free of charge and regardless of your plan”, through account settings or by contacting privacy@stackblitz.com, implemented within 15 days.
assessments.scope: Plan-invariant and explicitly free. Organisations may also opt out through administrator controls. Bolt Forge is governed separately by affirmative consent, and withdrawing consent does not necessarily stop use of content already contributed under it.
assessments.uncertainty: The control is documented even though the underlying default is not yet in effect. Having a switch is not the same as the default already suiting you.
assessments.plain: Yes — opt out at any time, free, on any plan, in account settings or by email.

assessments.claim: v0’s FAQ states that content of Enterprise customers “or any customer that has opted out of model training in their Vercel settings, is not used for training”, and directs users to change their Vercel team’s data preferences.
assessments.scope: Establishes a self-service route. It does not establish what each v0 subscription tier does by default.
assessments.uncertainty: Corrected. An earlier pass left this unresolved on an older tier-limited pricing table; the current FAQ describes the control without limiting it to a tier.
assessments.plain: Yes — turn training off in your Vercel team’s data settings.
assessments.condition: The setting lives in Vercel team settings rather than in v0 itself, so a team admin may need to make the change.
